title: Self-Paced Module: The Java Collections Framework

lessons.title: Beyond Arrays: The Java Collections Framework and the List Interface

objectives.cognitive: Explain the Java Collections Framework and the List interface, and distinguish an ArrayList from a LinkedList by how each stores and accesses its elements.
objectives.affective: Appreciate fairness in shared systems, such as a priority lane in a waiting line, and value organising information so that everyone is served in proper order.
objectives.psychomotor: Write and run a program that stores Vehicle objects in an ArrayList and manages a waiting line with a LinkedList.

blocks.markdown:
**Where we left off:** your folder should already have `Vehicle.java` (with `getCapacity()`, `board()`, and `quoteFare()`), `Jeepney.java`, `Tricycle.java`, `Bus.java`, `OverloadException.java`, and `InvalidDistanceException.java`. You will replace `Main.java` many times this week, so save a copy first as `Main_week13.txt`.

**No internet needed.** Keep every class in its own file, all in one folder. Compile with `javac *.java`, run with `java Main`.

**Why this week exists:** last week our fleet was an array of 3 (`Vehicle[] fleet = new Vehicle[3];`). An array's size is fixed when you create it, so a 4th jeepney simply does not fit. A collection grows and shrinks by itself, and comes with methods for adding, removing, searching, and sorting.

A **collection** is an object that holds a group of other objects. The **Java Collections Framework** is the set of ready-made interfaces (what a collection can do) and classes (working versions you can create with `new`) that Java gives you for storing, finding, and looping through groups of data. It lives in the `java.util` package.

A terminal manages its data in three different ways. The dispatcher's **logbook** lists trips in order, and the same jeepney can appear many times: that is a **List**. The LTO registration list names each plate number only once, with no repeats allowed: that is a **Set**. The **key cabinet** has a hook labelled with each plate number, so you find a key instantly by its label: that is a **Map**.

rows: Keeps order; allows duplicates; each item has an index 0, 1, 2…
the fleet; the line of waiting passengers
registered plates; stops on a route
Stores key → value pairs; each key appears once

blocks.markdown: **Reading the angle brackets:** a `List` of `Vehicle` is written with the type inside angle brackets after the word `List`. The type inside the brackets must be a class, so for numbers you write `Integer`, not `int`, and `Double`, not `double`. Java converts between them for you automatically.

lessons.title: No Duplicates Allowed: The Set Interface with HashSet and TreeSet

objectives.cognitive: Explain the Set interface's no-duplicate rule and distinguish a HashSet (no promised order) from a TreeSet (sorted order).
objectives.affective: Value accuracy and integrity in records, recognising that duplicate entries in real registries can cause unfairness and confusion.
objectives.psychomotor: Write and run programs that use a HashSet to refuse duplicate plate numbers and a TreeSet to list route stops in sorted order.

blocks.markdown: A **Set** is a collection that never holds the same item twice. If you try to add something already there, the set simply refuses and `add()` returns `false`. A Set has no index, so there is no `get(0)`.

The LTO will never register two vehicles with the same plate number. If someone tries to register NXA 123 again, the clerk says "already registered" and nothing changes. A Set behaves exactly like that clerk.

lessons.title: Find It by Its Key: The Map Interface with HashMap and TreeMap

objectives.cognitive: Explain the Map interface as key–value pairs with unique keys, and distinguish a HashMap from a TreeMap.
objectives.affective: Appreciate efficient organisation that saves other people's time, like a labelled key cabinet, and value orderly, findable records.
objectives.psychomotor: Write and run programs that look up vehicles in a HashMap, throwing a custom VehicleNotFoundException for a missing key, and that count trips in a TreeMap.

blocks.markdown: A **Map** stores pairs: a **key** and its **value**. You give the map a key, and it hands you the value instantly, without searching item by item. Each key can appear only once; putting a value under an existing key **replaces** the old value. A Map is part of the Collections Framework but is not a List or Set: it stores pairs, not single items.

The terminal's **key cabinet**: each hook has a label (the key: a plate number) and holds a jeepney key (the value). The dispatcher never searches every hook; she reads the label and takes the key. Two hooks can never have the same label.

blocks.markdown: **Why a custom exception?** `get()` on a missing key quietly returns `null`. If you then call `.showInfo()` on that `null`, the program crashes with a `NullPointerException`. `findVehicle()` checks with `containsKey()` first and throws a clear, checked exception instead, so whoever calls it is forced to plan for a missing plate. This is Week 13's lesson working inside this week's collections.

blocks.markdown: **What happened:** a for-each loop secretly uses an iterator to walk the list. When you changed the list behind its back with `fleet.remove(v)`, the iterator noticed the list had been modified while it was looping and stopped the program. Your line numbers may differ.

An **Iterator** is an object that walks through a collection one step at a time. `hasNext()` asks "is there another item?", `next()` moves to it, and `remove()` deletes the item you just visited. Because the iterator itself does the removing, it never loses its place.

performanceTask.title: Performance Task: Manage Your Data with Collections
performanceTask.markdown:
Open your own program from last week's Performance Task (your sari-sari store, pets, gadgets, school personnel, or shapes theme). Replace its arrays with collections, and add a List, a Set, and a Map that each do a real job. Start on Thursday after the Thursday exit slip; finish and present on Friday.

**Example (sari-sari store).** Do yours your own way:

- A Map of product to pieces in stock (a TreeMap, so the report is A to Z)
- A List of sales, in order, with repeats allowed
- A Set of customers, each counted once: adding Ana a second time is refused
- Sales today: 3 / Different customers: Ana, Ben

**Testing tip:** before you present, run your program at least four times: once normally, once adding a duplicate to your Set, once typing a key that exists, and once typing a key that does not exist. Every run must end with a friendly message, never an `Exception in thread "main"` report.

**Plan before you type** (show your teacher): for your List, Set, and Map write the class you will use, what it holds, and why this one and not the others. For your Iterator, write which items it will remove, and why.

**Schedule:** Thursday — Steps 7 to 10, the Thursday strip, then the plan and your List and Set. Friday — build the Map, the find method, and the loops; a classmate tries to break it; presentations and Q&A.
checklist: A List of your objects with at least 4, from at least 2 subclasses
A Set that refuses a duplicate — show add() returning false
A Map for looking up an object by a key (an ID, name, or code)
A find method that throws your own checked NotFound exception
Loop 1: an index for loop that numbers the items
Loop 2: a for-each loop that adds up or counts something
Loop 3: an Iterator that safely removes some items
The user types a key; a missing key shows a friendly message, never a crash
A comment on each part, e.g. // SET: no duplicate IDs
presentationOutline: Introduce your theme and your List, Set, and Map. (30 sec)
Run it: show the numbered list and the totals. (1 min)
Prove the rules live: add a duplicate to your Set; look up a key that exists and one that does not; remove items with your Iterator. (2 min)
Point to the code for each of the three loops and say why you chose it. (1 min)
questionsToPrepare: Why is your Set a Set and not a List?
What would change if your HashMap became a TreeMap?
What happens if you remove inside your for-each loop?
Why does your Map use Integer and not int?
Which loop could not work on your Set, and why?

rubric.criterion: List: holds at least 4 objects from at least 2 subclasses; uses add, get, size, and remove correctly
Set: fits a real must-be-unique rule; a duplicate is shown being refused
Map + exception: lookup by key works; a missing key throws the custom checked exception and is caught
Iteration: index for, for-each, and Iterator with remove each used for the right job; a Map loop with entrySet
Program quality: compiles and runs; no crash on bad input; parts labelled in comments
Presentation and Q&A: proves each rule live; explains every choice of collection and loop with own code
